items.question: Does any alternative path achieve coherence once this path is rejected?
premises: Everything established here fits coherently by this path.
Rejecting this path leaves no alternative framework.
No other proposed path attains logical coherence.
items.inference: Therefore the stated path alone is coherent and alternatives fail.
items.plain_english: Since everything established here fits together by this path, the whole system is coherent. If one rejects this path, surely no other approach attains any coherence at all.

items.question: How can initiation that cuts away impurities be possible in the dualist view?
premises: Initiation is defined as that which cuts away impurities.
The dualists hold a view of real difference.
The possibility of such cutting must be explained within that view.
items.inference: Initiation as removal of impurities is difficult to justify on the dualist position.
items.plain_english: For example, initiation is that which cuts away impurities; but how can this possibly be explained in the view of those who assert difference?

items.question: How can impurity cover a self whose nature is consciousness and all-pervading?
premises: Impurity is supposed to cover the self.
The self is of the nature of consciousness.
An all-pervading being cannot undergo a covering action.
items.inference: The covering of a conscious, all-pervading self by impurity is incoherent.
items.plain_english: For how can the so-called impurity cover a self whose nature is consciousness? And where is there any act of covering for an all-pervading being?

items.question: Can light ever be covered by darkness given light's nature?
premises: Light is never covered by darkness.
The arising of light is itself the act of destroying darkness.
What destroys darkness cannot be concealed by it.
items.inference: Consciousness, like light, cannot be covered by impurity.
items.plain_english: Light is never covered by darkness, because the very arising of light is an act that destroys darkness.

items.question: How can obstruction-type covering apply to an all-pervading being that does not move?
premises: Covering is defined as obstruction of something that moves, like rays.
The all-pervading self does not have motion.
Obstruction presupposes motion.
items.inference: Covering as obstruction cannot apply to the all-pervading self.
items.plain_english: Moreover, covering is said to be an obstruction of something that moves, like rays; so how could that apply to an all-pervading being that has no motion?

items.question: Is covering merely concealment of knowability rather than alteration of nature?
premises: Covering by a cloth conceals a pot's knowability.
Such covering does not alter the pot's own nature.
Concealment of knowability is distinct from change of essence.
items.inference: If covering means only concealment of knowability, it does not change the self's nature.
items.plain_english: Or else, covering is merely the concealment of knowability, as when a pot is covered by a cloth; it is not an alteration of its own nature.

items.question: Can selves of conscious nature be covered by concealment of knowability?
premises: Selves, being of the nature of consciousness, do not admit knowability as objects.
Covering as concealment of knowability presupposes object-knowability.
Applying such covering to selves is not even verbally coherent.
items.inference: The notion of covering selves by concealment of knowability is incoherent.
items.plain_english: But selves, because they are of the nature of consciousness, do not admit knowability; so to speak of their being covered is not fitting even in words.

items.question: If atomic selves are knowable to the Lord, does that contradict their conscious nature?
premises: An opponent claims the atomic selves are knowable to the Lord.
What is of the nature of consciousness is not an object of knowledge.
Making consciousness an object would conceal its conscious nature.
items.inference: The claim that conscious selves are knowable to the Lord is problematic.
items.plain_english: But surely, one objects, those atomic selves are knowable to the Lord. How so? For what is of the nature of consciousness is not knowable, since that would conceal its conscious nature.

items.question: What does the phrase 'awareness is knowable' resemble in its self-contradiction?
premises: The expression 'awareness is knowable' treats consciousness as an object.
This is like saying 'my mother is barren'.
Both expressions are internally self-contradictory.
items.inference: Calling consciousness knowable is a self-contradictory statement.
items.plain_english: The expression 'awareness is knowable' seems to recall its own fellow, the statement 'my mother is barren,' since both are self-contradictory.

items.question: Does the Lord's failure to know covered selves harm omniscience or the selves?
premises: If the Lord does not know covered atomic selves, his omniscience is impaired.
The selves themselves suffer no loss from not being known.
The problem falls on the doctrine of omniscience, not on the selves.
items.inference: The dualist account threatens the Lord's omniscience rather than explaining the selves' condition.
items.plain_english: Moreover, the Lord's omniscience would be impaired to that extent, because he would not know the covered atomic selves; yet there would be no harm to the selves themselves.

items.question: Does covering by impurity obstruct omniscience the way covering obstructs ordinary seeing?
premises: When a blue object is uncovered, the knower sees it; when covered, seeing does not occur.
By analogy, one might claim impurity obstructs omniscience.
The analogy assumes the knower is subject to obstruction.
items.inference: The opponent argues that impurity could obstruct even an omniscient knower by analogy with perception.
items.plain_english: But surely, when a blue object is uncovered the knower sees it, and when it is covered there is no seeing; likewise, one might say, an omniscient being covered by impurity would be obstructed.

items.question: Why does the perceptual analogy fail to show obstruction of the true knower?
premises: In ordinary perception, a cloth obstructs outgoing rays of sight.
The obstruction affects the rays, not the knower's essence.
There is no possibility of covering the conscious knower itself.
items.inference: The analogy from perception does not establish that the knower can be covered.
items.plain_english: Not so. In that case, a cloth obstructs the outgoing rays of sight, but there is no possibility of covering the knower himself.

items.question: Can a non-pervading impurity cover an all-pervading reality?
premises: Impurity is said to be non-pervading.
The self or consciousness is pervading.
A non-pervading thing cannot by its nature make an all-pervading space non-empty.
items.inference: A non-pervading impurity cannot coherently cover an all-pervading reality.
items.plain_english: It is clear that a non-pervading impurity cannot be the coverer of what is all-pervading; even in a pot, it would by its own nature make space non-empty only in a limited way.

items.question: If impurity produces no real effect on the self, how can it be capable of covering?
premises: The self is not subject to modification by impurity.
If impurity produces no effect, it cannot act on the self.
Covering requires the capacity to produce an effect.
items.inference: If impurity does not affect the self, it cannot coherently cover it.
items.plain_english: And if impurity produces no effect because the self is not subject to modification, how can it be capable of covering? Surely, sir, what then?

items.question: Is covering merely the bare coexistence of impurity with the atomic self?
premises: An opponent defines covering as the mere existence of impurity.
On this view, the atomic self is called covered simply by having impurity as a second.
This reduces covering to coexistence rather than an action.
items.inference: The opponent redefines covering as mere association with impurity.
items.plain_english: Indeed, its covering is said to be merely the existence of impurity; the atomic self is described as covered simply because it has impurity as a second.

items.question: Does defining covering as mere impurity-existence absurdly imply covering of Shiva?
premises: If covering is only the mere existence of impurity, the definition is too broad.
By that reasoning, even those of the stated nature could be said to have covering.
The definition would absurdly extend covering to Shiva.
items.inference: The mere-existence definition of covering leads to an absurd overextension.
items.plain_english: Alas, by this reasoning, even for those of the stated nature there would truly be a covering of Shiva, merely from the existence of impurity.

items.question: If the self covered by impurity does not know impurity, must another impurity be posited?
premises: A self covered by impurity would not know that impurity.
Non-awareness of impurity would itself need explanation.
Positing another impurity to explain this leads to regress.
items.inference: The covering account risks an infinite regress of impurities.
items.plain_english: Moreover, if the self covered by impurity does not even know the impurity, then in that non-awareness of it, is another impurity to be posited?

items.question: If the self knows impurity without vidya and kala, does that imply omniscience?
premises: An opponent suggests the self might simply know impurity.
Knowing impurity without vidya and kala would imply omniscience.
If impurity were known, the self could abandon it by various means.
items.inference: Allowing the self to know impurity directly creates further doctrinal problems.
items.plain_english: But what of it? Let it know the impurity. Then, without vidya and kala, there would be omniscience; and if the impurity were known, the self could abandon it by various contrived means.

items.question: If the self could abandon known impurity by contrived means, what covering would remain?
premises: If impurity were known, the self could abandon it by various contrived means.
Abandoning impurity would remove its covering effect.
This undermines the claim that impurity necessarily covers the self.
items.inference: The knowability of impurity would make its covering effect eliminable by the self.
items.plain_english: Let the self abandon it by those various contrived means; and if so, what covering would that impurity produce in the self?

items.question: How would the self become knower and doer of objects if impurity were removed by itself?
premises: Ordinary knowing and doing concern objects like pots.
The opponent appeals to vidya and kala as the basis of limited knowing and doing.
The question is how these arise if impurity alone explains bondage.
items.inference: The account of impurity must also explain the emergence of limited agency and knowledge.
uncertainties: The dual future form bhaviṣyataḥ is metrically/contextually unusual; taken as future sense.
items.plain_english: How would this self come to be a knower and doer with respect to pots and such things? Surely, one replies, because vidya and kala are held to be the basis of limited knowing and doing.

items.question: Who is deceived by the claim that inert maya and its products can manifest consciousness?
premises: Maya is of an inert nature.
Kala and the other limiting factors arise from maya.
Those with deluded understanding are misled by this account, not the wise.
items.inference: The dualist appeal to inert maya and its products is a deception for the deluded.
items.plain_english: In this way the deluded are deceived, but not the wise: this maya is inert by nature, and kala and the rest are its offspring.

items.question: How can the non-conscious manifest all-pervading consciousness with limiting qualities?
premises: What is non-conscious cannot manifest consciousness.
Consciousness is all-pervading.
Limiting qualities like finitude cannot properly qualify all-pervading consciousness.
items.inference: The dualist account cannot explain how inert factors manifest and limit consciousness.
items.plain_english: How could what is non-conscious be capable of manifesting consciousness? And if all-pervading consciousness were manifested, how could it be qualified by limitedness and such attributes?

items.question: Can the Lord manifest consciousness through kala and vidya if qualification suits only partite things?
premises: Being qualified is fitting only for things that have parts.
All-pervading consciousness is not partite.
An opponent suggests the Lord could manifest consciousness through kala and vidya.
items.inference: The appeal to divine manifestation through limiting instruments does not resolve the problem of qualifying consciousness.
items.plain_english: How could it become qualified? For that is fitting only for things that have parts. But surely, one objects, God, using kala and vidya, could manifest consciousness.

items.question: If God can manifest consciousness fully, why would liberation from eternal impurity be delayed?
premises: God could manifest consciousness in all ways without incapacity.
If impurity is eternal and God insists on it, liberation is unexplained.
Divine capacity and eternal bondage are in tension.
items.inference: The dualist account cannot explain delayed liberation if God is both capable and related to eternal impurity.
items.plain_english: Let him manifest it in all ways—alas, there is no incapacity in him. But if there is insistence on an eternal impurity, how will liberation ever come about?
